sources.title: RFC 8725 / BCP 225 — JSON Web Token Best Current Practices
RFC 9700 — Best Current Practice for OAuth 2.0 Security
PortSwigger Web Security Academy — JWT attacks
CVE-2015-9235 — node jsonwebtoken accepts HMAC-signed tokens where an asymmetric key was expected (fixed in 4.2.2)
Psychic Signatures in Java (CVE-2022-21449) — Neil Madden

structure.rationale: The book follows the shape of the trust question: first what a JWT physically is and what its signature does and does not promise (concepts 1-2), then the algorithm agreement that the whole guarantee rests on and the two ways it is subverted (3, 5), then the claim checks that turn a valid signature into a valid authorization decision (4), then the two problems that survive perfect cryptography — a token you cannot take back (6) and a token that escapes to somewhere it should not be (7) — closing with a checklist (8). Attack material precedes each defense so the mitigation reads as a consequence rather than a rule.
structure.audience: Backend and web developers who already ship JWTs but have never read RFC 7519 or 8725.

claims.text: A JWT in JWS Compact Serialization is three base64url-encoded parts separated by periods: the JOSE header, the claims set, and the signature.
The signature is computed over ASCII(BASE64URL(UTF8(protected header)) || '.' || BASE64URL(payload)) — the encoded header and payload, not the raw JSON.

Because the header is part of the signing input, a signature covers the algorithm declaration as well as the claims; RFC 7515 section 10.7 says applications should require alg to be carried in the protected header to prevent algorithm substitution.
The 'typ' header parameter declares the media type of the complete JWS and is ignored by JWS implementations — any processing of it is done by the application.

RFC 7519 section 7.2 gives a ten-step validation procedure: confirm the periods, decode and parse the JOSE header, confirm all header parameters are understood, determine whether the token is a JWS or JWE, verify it accordingly, handle nested JWTs recursively, then decode and validate the claims JSON.

snippets.note: RFC 7515 s.5.1 — what the signature actually covers

pitfalls: Reading claims from a decoded token before verifying its signature — every claim is attacker-controlled until the signature checks out.
Assuming 'typ: JWT' means anything is validated; the JWS layer ignores it.

claims.text: base64url is an encoding, not encryption: a JWS payload is readable by anyone holding the token, so a signed JWT provides integrity and authenticity but no confidentiality.
Confidentiality requires JWE, whose Compact Serialization has five parts, not three: protected header, encrypted key, initialization vector, ciphertext, and authentication tag.
A Nested JWT is a JWT used as the payload of an enclosing JWS or JWE; the 'cty' header must be set to 'JWT' in that case.

RFC 7519 section 11.2 states that when a token is both signed and encrypted, it must be signed first and then encrypted, to prevent signature stripping and to keep the signature itself from leaking information.
RFC 8725 sections 2.4 and 3.6 warn that compressing data before encryption can reveal plaintext information and say compression SHOULD NOT be done before encryption.

snippets.code:
# Anyone holding the token can read the payload — no key required.
cut -d. -f2 token.txt | base64 -d
snippets.note: demonstrates that a JWS payload is public

snippets.code: JWE = header . encrypted_key . iv . ciphertext . tag   (five parts)

pitfalls: Putting PII, internal role names, or anything you would not print on a postcard into a JWS payload.
Believing a long opaque-looking string is encrypted because it is unreadable to a human.

claims.text: RFC 7518 section 3.1 defines the JWS algorithms: HS256 is Required, RS256 and ES256 are Recommended (ES256 is Recommended+), the 384/512 variants and PS256/384/512 are Optional, and 'none' is Optional.

HMAC algorithms are symmetric — the same secret signs and verifies — while RS/ES/PS algorithms are asymmetric, so verifiers need only the public key. This difference is what makes key distribution safe and what makes algorithm confusion possible.
RFC 7518 section 3.2 requires an HMAC key at least as large as the hash output — 256 bits for HS256 — and section 3.3 requires RSA keys of 2048 bits or larger.
RFC 7515 section 10.1 recommends a minimum of 128 bits of entropy for all keys.
RFC 8725 section 2.2 and 3.5 warn that human-memorable passwords must not be used directly as MAC keys; weak HMAC secrets are brute-forcible offline from a single captured token.

The 'none' algorithm produces an Unsecured JWS with no integrity protection; RFC 7518 section 3.6 says implementations MUST NOT accept Unsecured JWSs by default, and RFC 8725 section 3.2 says libraries should not generate them without an explicit request.
alg:none filters have been bypassed by case variation such as 'None' or 'nOnE', because the check was a string comparison rather than an allow-list of expected algorithms.
RFC 8725 section 3.2 recommends deterministic ECDSA per RFC 6979 and advises against RSA PKCS#1 v1.5 encryption padding in favour of RSAES-OAEP.

CVE-2022-21449 ('Psychic Signatures', Java 15-18) made ECDSA verification accept a signature whose r and s values were both zero, because the implementation failed to reject zero values — an all-zero signature verified against any key until the April 2022 patch.

snippets.note: the Unsecured JWS header; the third part of the token is empty

snippets.code:
// The fix CVE-2015-9235 forced: pin the algorithms, do not read them from the token.
jwt.verify(token, publicKey, { algorithms: ['RS256'] })

pitfalls: Treating the header's alg as an instruction rather than as an untrusted claim to be checked against a server-side allow-list.
Using a memorable string such as 'secret' or an app name as an HS256 key.
Assuming a well-known library or platform verifies correctly — CVE-2015-9235 and CVE-2022-21449 both broke verification itself.

claims.text: Every registered claim in RFC 7519 section 4.1 — iss, sub, aud, exp, nbf, iat, jti — is optional; the specification defines their meaning, not their presence, so an application must require the ones it depends on.
'exp' (4.1.4) is a NumericDate after which the JWT MUST NOT be accepted, and 'nbf' (4.1.5) is one before which it MUST NOT be accepted; the spec permits a small leeway for clock skew.

'aud' (4.1.3) identifies the recipients the JWT is intended for and may be a single StringOrURI or an array; RFC 8725 section 3.9 requires the relying party to validate it when several parties share an issuer.
'jti' (4.1.7) is a unique identifier for the token, intended to let a recipient detect replay.

RFC 8725 section 3.8 requires applications to verify that the cryptographic key used actually belongs to the claimed issuer and to reject the token otherwise — verifying a signature with the wrong issuer's key is a valid signature and an invalid decision.
RFC 8725 sections 2.7 and 3.8-3.9 describe substitution attacks, where a token legitimately issued for one recipient is replayed at another; issuer and audience validation is the defense.

RFC 8725 sections 2.8 and 3.11-3.12 describe cross-JWT confusion, where a token of one kind (say an ID token) is accepted where another kind (an access token) was expected; the mitigation is explicit typing with a 'typ' header such as 'application/example+jwt' plus mutually exclusive validation rules.
RFC 8725 section 3.3 requires that all cryptographic operations in the JWT be validated, including those in nested JWTs.
RFC 8725 sections 2.6 and 3.7 require UTF-8 for the JSON and rejection of other Unicode encodings, to prevent divergent interpretation of the same bytes.
RFC 9700 section 2.3 recommends that access tokens SHOULD be audience-restricted to a specific resource server, or to a small set of them.

snippets.note: the shape of a complete verification call: algorithm, issuer, audience, bounded skew

pitfalls: Calling a decode() function that parses without verifying and treating the result as authenticated.
Checking exp but not aud, so any token from the same issuer opens every service behind it.
Allowing generous clock skew (minutes or hours), which extends the life of every stolen token by the same amount.

claims.text: Algorithm confusion: an attacker changes alg from RS256 to HS256 and signs the forged token using the server's RSA public key as the HMAC secret; a server that selects its verification algorithm from the token's own header then verifies the forgery successfully, because the public key is a value the attacker also holds.

CVE-2015-9235 (CVSS 9.8) was exactly this flaw in node's jsonwebtoken before 4.2.2: verify() accepted the algorithm from the token header by default. The fix introduced an explicit algorithms option; pinning algorithms: ['RS256'] makes the swap impossible.

The 'kid' header (RFC 7515 section 4.1.4) is a hint indicating which key was used, with unspecified structure — so it is attacker-controlled input that frequently reaches a filesystem path or SQL query. RFC 8725 section 3.10 requires validating or sanitizing it.

kid path traversal has been used to point verification at a predictable file such as /dev/null, giving an empty key the attacker can sign with; kid values interpolated into SQL have yielded injection.

The 'jku' header names a URL from which to fetch the JWK Set; a server that fetches it without an allow-list can be pointed at an attacker-hosted key set, and the fetch itself is an SSRF primitive. RFC 8725 section 3.10 requires whitelisting jku and x5u URLs.

The 'jwk' header embeds the public key in the token itself; a server that trusts it verifies the attacker's signature against the attacker's own key. PortSwigger's stated defense is a limited allow-list of public keys.
RFC 7515 section 4.1 requires that jku and x5u resources be acquired over TLS with a validated server identity, providing integrity protection for the retrieved keys.

snippets.note: both degrees of freedom belong to the attacker
kid never becomes a path or a query

pitfalls: Passing the token's own alg into the verify call.
Using kid to build a filename, a URL, or a SQL string.
Fetching keys from jku or x5u without a host allow-list.

claims.text: A verified JWT is valid because its signature and claims check out, not because a server says so — so a stateless deployment has nothing to consult when a token must be withdrawn, and the token stays good until exp.
The practical mitigations are: short access-token lifetimes, a denylist keyed on jti for the remaining window, and a stateful refresh step that can be revoked centrally.

RFC 9700 section 2.2.2 requires that refresh tokens for public clients be sender-constrained or use refresh token rotation; section 4.14 details both mechanisms as protection against stolen refresh tokens.
Refresh token rotation means each use issues a new refresh token and invalidates the old one, so a replayed old token signals theft and lets the issuer revoke the whole chain.
'jti' exists precisely so a recipient can identify a specific token, which is what makes per-token revocation possible without abandoning the format.

snippets.code:
access token   5-15 min, stateless, verified locally
refresh token  long-lived, stateful, rotated on every use, revocable
logout         delete the refresh record + denylist outstanding jti until exp
snippets.note: the standard split that makes logout mean something

pitfalls: Shipping 24-hour or 30-day access tokens because re-authentication felt inconvenient.
Building a denylist and never expiring entries, so it grows without bound; entries only need to live until the token's own exp.
Believing 'stateless auth' means no server-side session state anywhere — the revocable part has to live somewhere.

claims.text: A bearer token is a password with an expiry date: anyone who holds it can use it, so every place a copy comes to rest is part of the attack surface.

Tokens placed in URLs leak through browser history, Referer headers, server access logs, and shared links; RFC 9700 section 2.1.2 discourages the implicit grant for exactly this class of access-token exposure, recommending the authorization code flow instead.

Tokens in localStorage are readable by any JavaScript running on the origin, so a single XSS becomes token theft; OWASP's long-standing guidance is not to store session identifiers in local storage because the data is always accessible to JavaScript.

An HttpOnly cookie is not readable by JavaScript, which blocks the direct theft path, but it is attached automatically by the browser and therefore needs CSRF defenses — SameSite, a custom header, or a double-submit token.

RFC 8725 sections 2.9 and 3.10 warn against blindly trusting claims used in lookups: values from a token that reach logs, queries, or outbound requests must be sanitized like any other untrusted input.
RFC 9700 section 2.3 and 4.10.2 recommend audience-restricting access tokens so that a token stolen from one resource server cannot be replayed at another.

snippets.note: why tokens in URLs are a leak class of their own

snippets.code: Set-Cookie: session=<jwt>; HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Lax; Path=/
snippets.note: blocks JS read; still requires CSRF thinking

pitfalls: Logging the Authorization header, or a whole request object that contains it, at debug level.
Storing an access token in localStorage 'temporarily' and never revisiting it.
Treating XSS as a lower-severity bug on a site that keeps tokens in JavaScript-reachable storage.

claims.text: The minimum server-side checks are: pin the algorithm allow-list, resolve the key without trusting token-supplied locations, verify the signature before reading any claim, then require iss, aud, and exp with bounded clock skew.
RFC 8725 section 3.1 requires libraries to let callers specify supported algorithms and to verify that the header algorithm matches the operation performed.
RFC 8725 section 3.11 recommends explicit typing via the 'typ' header, in the form 'application/example+jwt', to keep different kinds of token from being interchangeable.
RFC 7518 minimum key sizes: HMAC keys at least the hash output size (256 bits for HS256); RSA keys 2048 bits or larger.

snippets.code:
1 pin alg   2 resolve key server-side   3 verify signature   4 exp/nbf + skew
5 iss       6 aud                       7 typ                8 revocation path
snippets.note: the checklist order — each step's output is the next step's precondition

pitfalls: Treating the checklist as advisory: every item on it corresponds to a published, exploited failure.
